title: Customer-edge NAT handshake & audit playbook (PRD sketch)
content:
Context and problem statement:

We often onboard customers who operate their own edge gateways / NATs between their VPC and Redwood Private components. Network-level changes on the customer side (NAT port mappings, egress ACLs, SG rules, and gateway restarts) are the most common root cause of transient failures and outages in private deployments.

Goal of this doc:
- Define a lightweight, deterministic handshake ("NAT handshake") that runs during onboarding and when network changes are detected, producing compact, verifiable audit artifacts for our approval gates and SRE troubleshooting.
- Propose log formats, sampling rules, and UX for approval gates when we ask customers to make configuration changes.
- Surface operational tradeoffs (latency, evidence size, privacy) and a minimal implementation plan.

Non-goals:
- Replace customer-side logging systems or SIEM.
- Full cryptographic attestation of third-party devices (out of scope for MVP).

High-level approach:
1) Minimal handshake layer: a small exchange between a Redwood switch/proxy and a customer edge agent (or NAT device) that records reachability and translation state.
2) Compact evidence artifact: JSON lines (one event per line) containing: timestamp, observed source/destination tuple, NAT-mapped port, observed TTL/seq fingerprint, and a short base64-encoded packet-sample hash. No raw payload.
3) Approval gate integration: when a proposed network change is submitted (via ticket / Console flow), the system requests a targeted handshake snapshot covering the affected IP/ports, stores the artifact, and flags the change for human review if anomalies are present.

Handshake sequence (MVP):
- Trigger: onboarding or explicit change request (Console/Operator API) OR anomaly detection (failed health checks, symmetric NAT visible).
- Step A: Redwood initiates a non-invasive TCP/UDP probe to a negotiated ephemeral port on the customer edge. Probe metadata includes a short nonce and TTL probe pattern.
- Step B: Customer edge agent responds with a tiny signed ACK (HMAC using a pre-shared onboarding token) containing the observed mapping and timestamp. If the device cannot sign, return a plain ACK with a confidence score.
- Step C: Both sides log the exchange as a single event; both sides also compute a short digest of the packet-sample.

Event schema (compact line-based JSON, one-per-handshake):
- id: uuid-v4
- ts_utc: ISO-8601
- direction: inbound|outbound
- src: ip:port (observed by Redwood)
- dst: ip:port (observed by Redwood)
- nat_mapping: ip:port (if different)
- probe_type: tcp_syn|udp_probe|icmp
- probe_nonce: base64url
- responder_token_id: friendly-id (customer token alias)
- signature_present: true|false
- sample_hash: sha256(base64-trimmed)
- confidence: low|medium|high
- note: free text (optional)

Privacy constraints and minimalization: we explicitly avoid capturing packet payloads. sample_hash is computed over the 64 byte IP/TCP header window only, then truncated to 16 bytes and base64url encoded — enough to correlate but not reconstruct. Artifacts stored in Redwood are encrypted at rest and access-limited to SRE/ProdOps and CS representatives for the customer under the existing Private data access policy.

Approval gate flow (console + human ops):
- Customer initiates change request in Console or via support ticket (linked to JIRA).
- Console auto-requests a narrow handshake snapshot (timebox: 30s) and displays a short summary: mapping observed, confidence, last-seen delta.
- If mapping or observed endpoints deviate from expected (policy rules), flag for human review. Reviewer sees: artifact id, time window, obfuscated src/dst, and a short explanation heuristic (e.g., "ephemeral port range outside expected 60000-61000").
- Reviewer options: Approve, Request re-check (re-run handshake), Escalate to SRE, Reject (block config change in Console). All actions are recorded in the change-approval ledger with links to the artifact.

Sampling & retention strategy:
- We avoid capturing handshake artifacts for every packet. Sampling rules:
  - onboarding and explicit change ops: 100% snapshot for the affected flows for 60s
  - anomaly-triggered: 1 in N progressive sampling (N configurable per-customer; default N=5)
  - continuous telemetry: aggregate counters only (no per-handshake samples)
- Retention:
  - Full handshake artifacts kept for 90 days for customers on enterprise plans; 14 days for standard private tenants.
  - Summaries (non-identifying metrics) kept for 2 years for capacity and risk modeling.

UX & Console concerns (notes):
- Present summaries in human-friendly terms; avoid exposing raw IPs by default (show obfuscated mask, with a "reveal" control that requires 2FA and a justification note).
- Make re-run button obvious — many network flaps are intermittent. Avoid forcing the reviewer to chase a stale snapshot.

Operational playbook (quick ops steps):
- When a customer reports a transient error after a config change, run: handshake(retry=3, interval=5s) -> collect artifacts -> diff against baseline artifact (onboarding snapshot) -> produce decision card for approval gate.
- If signatures absent: increase sampling and request out-of-band customer confirmation (Slack/email ticket).

Risk & open questions (MVP scope):
- Q: How do we authenticate the edge agent? A: MVP uses onboarding shared tokens (rotatable). Longer term we should integrate with customer KMS or mutual TLS with customer-managed certs.
- Q: Can malicious customers spoof artifacts? A: Without cryptographic attestation, artifacts are best-effort evidence. We rely on cross-correlation with telemetry and operator confirmation for high-risk approvals.
- Q: Regulatory concerns about retention of metadata (EU PII laws)? A: We will consult Legal; minimize retention and offer opt-out/shorter retention for regulated customers.

Implementation plan (MVP roadmap):
- Spike 1 (2w): implement PoC handshake agent & small Redwood probe harness (local sim environment). Ticket: JIRA-3507.
- Spike 2 (3w): event schema + storage prototype in secure blob store, console summary UI mock. JIRA-3510.
- Beta (6w): integrate with approval flow, sampling config per-tenant, add access control checks and audit trails. JIRA-3526.
- Rollout: opt-in beta customers -> measure false positive/negative rates -> iterate on confidence heuristics (TTL, seq fingerprinting).

Notes to reviewers / TODOs:
- Jonah: can you add a sketch of the probe packet format and HMAC mechanics?
- Leah: UX microcopy for the Console modal (obfuscation/reveal flow).
- Ravi: confirm storage encryption knobs we should use and draft retention opt-in language.
- Ops: define the baseline diff criteria (what constitutes "significant deviation").

References and links:
- onboarding-cookbook Confluence (linked above)
- internal test harness: github.com/redwood-inference/test-edge-harness (WIP)
- Similar idea: see external paper on lightweight network provenance (cite in final PRD).

Short example artifact (single line, illustrative):
{"id":"e3f2a7c4-9f1d-4b6a-b0c3-5a2e7f9a1a2b","ts_utc":"2026-02-15T18:22:07Z","direction":"inbound","src":"198.51.100.23:52344","dst":"10.0.0.5:8080","nat_mapping":"35.196.8.77:52344","probe_type":"tcp_syn","probe_nonce":"k3f2sQ","responder_token_id":"cust-alpha-01","signature_present":false,"sample_hash":"q1X7m4dL3pZQ8fA1","confidence":"medium","note":"ephemeral port outside expected range"}

This is a working sketch. Goal is to get a small, testable artifact that helps us make approval decisions faster and gives SREs the forensic hooks they need without storing excessive customer data.
